stories.title: Apollo, BDT & MSD Partners Provide $197M to Build Naples Luxury Condos
stories.excerpt: Kolter Urban and BH Group have secured $197 million in construction financing to build Olana Naples Residences, an estate-style condominium residence in Naples, Fla., along Florida’s Gulf Coast, Commercial Observer can first report. Apollo Global Management and BDT & MSD Partners provided the debt. No broker was listed on the transaction. Located at 1121 Gulf Shore Boulevard North in Naples — the beachside city on the western shores of Florida and self-styled “Golf Capital of the World” — Olana Naples Residences will deliver 12 estate-style condominiums spanning 10,000 square feet each. The lowest priced residence will enter the market at $32 million. The developers plan to break ground before 2026 is out, with a timeline to complete construction by 2028. Kolter Urban and BH Group did not respond to requests for comment. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Apollo, BDT & MSD closed $197M construction financing for Olana Naples Residences.
12 estate condos averaging 10,000 SF, $32M entry price, Gulf Shore Boulevard North.
Groundbreaking targeted end of 2025, delivery 2028; luxury product in supply-constrained market.
stories.summary: Kolter Urban and BH Group secured $197 million in construction debt from Apollo Global Management and BDT & MSD Partners to build Olana Naples Residences in Naples, Florida—an ultra-luxury estate-style condominium project with 12 units averaging 10,000 square feet each, priced from $32 million. The developers plan to break ground before 2026 closes and complete by 2028. This is a high-barrier-to-entry luxury product with minimal unit count, targeting affluent buyers seeking Gulf Coast waterfront estates.
stories.impact: This capital deployment signals strong investor appetite for luxury resort-market real estate, but the ultra-high price point ($32M+) and limited unit count (12 total) create minimal demand spillover into workforce or market-rate multifamily. The financing structure and sponsors reflect confidence in high-net-worth migration to Naples, which may accelerate service-sector and support-labor demand—a secondary signal for workforce housing needs in the Naples metro, but not a direct demand driver for TCR's core multifamily product.

stories.title: 333 N. Central Office Investor Snags $44.5M Financing
stories.excerpt: Foundation 8 and Hilco Global Real Estate Capital closed a $44.5 million loan secured by the office component of 333 N Central Avenue, a mixed-use tower in Downtown Phoenix. The financed property comprises 246,490 square feet of Class AA office space across the top eight floors of the tower, 2,522 square feet of ground-floor retail space, rooftop amenity rights, and shared access to the building’s parking structure. A separately owned 242-key Westin Hotel occupies the middle portion of the building. The financing will support Foundation 8’s repositioning of the office space from a historically single-tenant corporate headquarters into a signature multi-tenant office property. It was originally built for Freeport-McMoRan. Foundation 8 has engaged Newmark to lead the leasing effort. Hilco Global structured the $44.5 million first mortgage financing to refinance existing acquisition financing and provide additional capital to support leasing costs, tenant improvements, capital improvements, and other costs associated with the execution of Foundation 8’s business plan. The post 333 N. Central Office Investor Snags $44.5M Financing appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Foundation 8 refinanced 246,490 SF Class AA office at 333 N Central Avenue, Phoenix, via $44.5M loan.
Converting single-tenant corporate HQ (Freeport-McMoRan) into multi-tenant signature office property.
Hilco Global structured first mortgage to fund leasing, TI, and capital improvements.
stories.summary: Foundation 8 and Hilco Global Real Estate Capital closed a $44.5 million first-mortgage loan against the office component of 333 N Central Avenue in Downtown Phoenix. The Class AA space spans 246,490 square feet across the top eight floors of this mixed-use tower (which also includes a separately owned 242-key Westin Hotel and retail). The financing refinances acquisition debt and provides capital for leasing costs, tenant improvements, and repositioning from single-tenant corporate headquarters into multi-tenant office.
stories.impact: This refinance reflects capital market appetite for adaptive-use office-to-multi-tenant conversions in core urban markets, but does not directly affect multifamily development in Phoenix. However, the successful repositioning and lender confidence in Downtown Phoenix mixed-use assets signals broader market stabilization in that submarket, which may improve financing availability and cap rates for adjacent or future residential components in similar urban-core projects.

stories.title: W Hotels to Take 9 Floors of 400 South Tryon
stories.excerpt: Spandrel Development Partners announced plans for W Hotels to come to uptown Charlotte as the hospitality anchor of 400 South Tryon. The 200-key hotel, which will feature 173 guest rooms and 27 suites. It is being developed in partnership with 7G Group. 400 South Tryon is a 32-story high-rise that was formerly the Wachovia Center. The hotel will span floors 1 through 9 of the building, with a signature rooftop food-and-beverage venue on the 34th floor. Plans also call for 12,000 square feet of meeting space, a ground-floor restaurant and coffee bar, ballroom and pre-function space, and the brand’s signature Living Room experience. The mixed-use project will transform the former 1970s office tower into a new destination combining the 200-key hotel with 399 unbranded studio, one-, two and three-bedroom residences. Residential amenities will include an indoor pool, wellness-focused spa and fitness center, theater room, golf simulator, and esident lounges. The hotel will be designed by Rockwell Group, with LS3P serving as architect of record.  The post W Hotels to Take 9 Floors of 400 South Tryon appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: W Hotels signed to anchor 400 South Tryon, Charlotte uptown; 200 keys across floors 1–9.
Mixed-use conversion: 200-key hotel + 399 residential units (studios to 3BR), 32-story former Wachovia Center.
Residences include pool, spa, fitness, theater, golf simulator; Rockwell Group/LS3P design.
stories.summary: Spandrel Development Partners and 7G Group announced a 200-key W Hotels at 400 South Tryon, uptown Charlotte, occupying floors 1–9 of a 32-story former office tower. The mixed-use project will also include 399 unbranded residential units (studios and one- to three-bedroom apartments) with amenities including pool, wellness spa, fitness, theater, and golf simulator. The hotel features a signature rooftop F&B venue on the 34th floor, ground-floor restaurant, and 12,000 SF of meeting space.
stories.impact: This redevelopment catalyzes uptown Charlotte residential demand by co-locating hotel and apartment uses, creating lifestyle amenities and urban activation that increase renter appeal and pricing power for the 399-unit residential component. The mixed-use format—particularly the hotel-driven foot traffic and shared amenities—supports market-rate rent growth in uptown Charlotte and validates infill density in the submarket. For TCR, this signals strong capital backing for dense urban residential conversion projects in Charlotte, an emerging growth market, and the viability of amenity-heavy lifestyle positioning.

stories.title: Greystar, PGIM Complete Phase I of Charleston Warehouse Project
stories.excerpt: Greystar and PGIM, the global asset management business of Prudential Financial, completed Lowcountry Logistics Center Building I and began construction of Buildings II and III in the greater Charleston area. The 145,463-square-foot rear-loading facility at 7651 Southrail Road has a clear height of 32 feet, 34 dock doors, and two drive-in doors. Leasing efforts are being led by Peter Fennelly, Simons Johnson and Will Crowell of Bridge Commercial. Construction is underway on Lowcountry Logistics Buildings II and III, located at 8276 & 8250 Patriot Boulevard in North Charleston. The two rear-load buildings total over 180,000 square feet. All three buildings can accommodate a wide range of industrial users, with suites divisible to approximately 16,000 square feet and are well suited for distribution, warehousing and manufacturing operations. Hagood S. Morrison, John Beam, Brooks Courtney, and Graham Weisel of Bridge Commercial will lead leasing efforts for Buildings II and III. The post Greystar, PGIM Complete Phase I of Charleston Warehouse Project appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Greystar and PGIM completed Lowcountry Logistics Building I (145,463 SF) in greater Charleston area.
Buildings II and III under construction (180,000+ SF total) on Patriot Boulevard, North Charleston.
Rear-load, 32-foot clear height, 34 dock doors; divisible to ~16,000 SF; Bridge Commercial leasing.
stories.summary: Greystar and PGIM (Prudential Financial's asset management arm) completed the first building of Lowcountry Logistics Center in the greater Charleston area—a 145,463-square-foot rear-loading facility with 32-foot clear height, 34 dock doors, and flexible suites. Phase II and III buildings (180,000+ SF combined) are under construction on Patriot Boulevard in North Charleston. All three buildings target distribution, warehousing, and manufacturing tenants with divisible units down to approximately 16,000 square feet.
stories.impact: This logistics center expansion reflects strong capital confidence in Charleston's industrial/supply-chain infrastructure, driven by regional port growth and distribution demand. While primarily industrial, the project signals job growth and employer investment in the Charleston metro that will drive underlying apartment demand—particularly for workforce and value-add multifamily near logistics hubs in North Charleston, a submarket experiencing supply-chain tenant influx and rent growth.

stories.title: Longpoint Pays $195M for 10-Building Miami Warehouse Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Longpoint Partners acquired a 10-building industrial portfolio in Miami-Dade County for $195 million. The portfolio comprises 729,901 square feet on approximately 41.8 acres in established Miami industrial submarkets. The seller’s name was not disclosed. At acquisition, the portfolio was 90% occupied by 74 tenants, with an average tenant size of approximately 9,864 square feet. The 10 buildings average approximately 72,990 square feet and offer clear heights ranging from 17 to 25 feet, 231 loading positions, front and rear loading configurations, and a 40% floor area ratio. These characteristics provide flexible space for a broad range of industrial users and align with Longpoint’s focus on functional assets in supply-constrained infill locations. Longpoint acquired the portfolio for approximately $267 per square foot. The firm maintains offices in Miami and Fort Lauderdale. Longpoint added Miami’s population growth, proximity to major consumer markets and critical transportation infrastructure continue to support demand for well-located industrial space. The post Longpoint Pays $195M for 10-Building Miami Warehouse Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Longpoint Partners acquired 10-building Miami-Dade industrial portfolio for $195M (729,901 SF).
90% occupied by 74 tenants; $267 per SF; 41.8 acres, 17–25 foot clear heights, 231 loading positions.
Functional infill assets in supply-constrained locations; Longpoint offices in Miami and Fort Lauderdale.
stories.summary: Longpoint Partners bought a 10-building industrial portfolio in Miami-Dade County for $195 million, comprising 729,901 square feet across 41.8 acres in established submarkets. At acquisition, the portfolio was 90% occupied by 74 tenants, averaging 9,864 square feet per tenant. Buildings offer clear heights of 17–25 feet, 231 loading positions, front and rear loading, and a 40% floor-area ratio. Longpoint paid approximately $267 per square foot for supply-constrained infill functional assets.
stories.impact: This $195M acquisition validates Miami-Dade industrial scarcity and pricing power, reflecting structural supply constraints and sustained demand from e-commerce and regional distribution. The deal signals capital competition for industrial assets but does not directly drive multifamily demand. However, the employment and logistics-sector investment in Miami-Dade—combined with the metro's population growth—underpins long-term apartment demand in secondary and value-add submarkets closer to industrial corridors, particularly for workforce-focused communities.

stories.title: Texas People & Companies, September 11, 2026
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield announced today that Heinrich Cronje has joined the firm as Managing Director in the firm’s Houston Healthcare Advisory Practice. Cronje specializes in healthcare real estate and brings a broad range of commercial real estate experience to Cushman & Wakefield. His practice includes representation of healthcare tenants as well as leading health systems, institutional and entrepreneurial owners of medical office properties and other sophisticated healthcare owners, operators and investors. Over the course of his brokerage career, he has closed healthcare transactions valued at more than $300 million. Northmarq has added a Houston-based retail investment sales team consisting of longtime partners Matt Berry, Robbie Kilcrease, and Drew Reinking. Formerly directors of CBRE’s Texas Retail Investment Sales group, Berry, Kilcrease and Reinking join Northmarq as managing directors and members of the National Shopping Center Group, strengthening the firm’s coast-to-coast retail offering and expanding its capabilities across Texas. Weitzman hired financial executive Douglas (Doug) Nash, MBA, CPA, as its Chief Financial Officer. In this position, Nash will manage the company’s finances, assess financial risks and opportunities, and set and track financial goals, objectives and budgets. Most recently, he served as the CFO for The Retail Connection, a Dallas-based retail real estate services firm, where he was responsible for the finance | accounting, treasury, information technology and property management divisions. Welcome Group, a Houston-based commercial real estate investor and developer focused on manufacturing, laboratory, warehouse and distribution facilities, today announced the addition of five professionals to its team. Rob Canizalez has joined Welcome Group as Senior Property Manager, Sabrina Hollis as Property Manager, Gillian Boyer as Operational Accounting Director and Wesley Hightower as Finance Manager. William Hirtz

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Teresa Minnick of Christie’s International Real Estate Group
stories.excerpt: Move over “Jersey Boys,” because this Jersey girl is the queen bee of the New Jersey real estate market. Teresa Minnick of Christie’s International Real Estate Group is a leading broker in the Garden state, with a career spanning over 25 years and boasting more than $800 million in sales. Minnick has added many a feather to her cap over the course of her career, with several standout projects, including her work in Asbury Park and a luxury condominium project in Long Branch at the Atlantic Club Residences. And her work stays focused at the Jersey Shore, where she said she finds peace in the “history, architecture and charm,” as well as the beautiful oceanfront homes. Commercial Observer caught up with Minnick in early September for a series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career? Teresa Minnick: The Atlantic Club Residences — a landmark 132-residence luxury oceanfront development in Long Branch, N.J., with approximately $200 million in current sales. Being part of a project of this scale, from pre-construction through what will ultimately become an extraordinary new oceanfront community, has been an incredible experience. What is your career Everest? Being part of the transformation of Asbury Park during the real estate crash. I had the opportunity to work alongside visionaries who believed in bringing the City by the Sea back to life at a time when many people couldn’t yet see its potential. Watching that vision become a reality — and knowing I played a part in it — remains one of the most rewarding chapters of my career. Who has been your biggest influence? My mentors, Carol Blasucci, Lee Bossie (“Aunt Gigi”), and Al Garfall. Al, formerly of SGS Communities and D.R. Horton and currently with Lennar, was one of the people who helped shape the way I approach real est

It reflects strong sales velocity in Jersey Shore luxury condo market, but offers no signal on supply, demand, underwriting, or capital availability relevant to TCR's development pipeline.

stories.title: One Generation’s Senior Housing Boom Is Another’s Bust
stories.excerpt: Today’s senior housing boom comes with an expiration date, and the developers who recognize that now will hold the long-term competitive advantage. The financial engine powering this boom is a single-generation phenomenon. Those continuing to build exclusively for the top of the market are making a bet the demographics likely don’t support. The defining strategic questions of the next decade revolve around rethinking capital stacks, product design, and who the market should build for. Senior housing occupancy is projected to reach 90 percent by the end of 2026, and transaction volume is up more than 40 percent year-over-year. The momentum is undeniable, but so are the underlying demographics. The next generation of American seniors cannot afford what the market is currently building. Nicole De Bare. PHOTO: Courtesy HSF Kramer Baby boomers hold more than $85 trillion in wealth — over half of all U.S. household net worth — built over decades of home equity appreciation, widespread pension access and sustained market gains. Boomers had time on their side: decades of compounding wealth growth, broad access to employer-guaranteed pensions that largely no longer exist, and a long run of rising asset values. They are, by nearly every financial measure, the most retirement-ready generation in American history. They are also the most active. Today’s boomer seniors are entering retirement healthier and more lifestyle-oriented than any generation before them, fueling demand not just for housing, but also for communities built around fitness, social engagement and continued independence. That lifestyle comes at a price. Premium communities offering resort-style amenities, wellness programming and curated social environments remain squarely out of reach for anyone without significant financial resources. Developers have cashed in on the “silver tsunami,” but future generations likely won’t catch the same wave — even as that wave only grows larger. T
bullets: Senior housing occupancy projected 90% by end 2026; transaction volume up 40% YoY.
Baby boomers hold $85T wealth (>50% of U.S. household net worth); Gen X lacks equivalent wealth/pensions.
Strategic shift needed: current luxury-only product mix unsustainable; future demand requires affordable, diverse senior housing.
stories.summary: Senior housing is experiencing a cyclical boom driven by baby boomer wealth ($85 trillion, over half of all U.S. household net worth), with occupancy projected to reach 90% by end 2026 and transaction volume up over 40% year-over-year. However, the underlying demographics do not support indefinite high-end-only development. Generation X, the next cohort of seniors, lacks the pension access, home-equity appreciation runway, and sustained market gains that enabled boomer wealth accumulation. Developers betting exclusively on top-of-market senior housing are structuring for a single-generation phenomenon and will face headwinds as demographic demand shifts.
stories.impact: This analysis signals a structural ceiling on luxury senior housing demand circa 2030 and a looming market transition toward mid-market and affordable senior housing. For TCR, this means growth opportunities in senior-inclusive multifamily or senior-oriented value-add renovation projects targeting Gen X affordability profiles will outperform luxury-only senior builds. Capital stack innovation, inclusive product design, and early positioning in mid-market senior housing in growing metros will define competitive advantage in the next decade; pure-play luxury senior development carries refinance and lease-up risk post-2028.

stories.title: Friedman’s Restaurant Ownership Buys Upper West Side Retail Space to Open New Spot
stories.excerpt: The ownership group behind famed New York City restaurants Friedman’s Restaurant and Pastrami Queen has acquired a retail co-op on Manhattan’s Upper West Side to open a new eatery, Commercial Observer has learned. The restaurant group, using the LLC Mountain View Acquisition, bought the 5,000-square-foot retail unit at 541-555 Amsterdam Avenue for $4.1 million, according to buyer representative Lee & Associates NYC. The site is currently home to Barney Greengrass, a longtime Upper West Side restaurant and fish vendor, and Hudson & Charles, a butcher shop that also sells sandwiches and groceries. Both businesses will remain in their current locations following the completion of the sale, according to Lee. The new buyer plans to open another Friedman’s Restaurant location in the retail co-op’s existing vacant unit. There are at least seven Friedman’s locations in Manhattan already, including its first-ever location at Chelsea Market. The chain offers a variety of eats and spirits, including breakfast classics, sandwiches and burgers. “The group is expanding its footprint in a top location on the Upper West Side, while also keeping a New York institution intact and operating for years to come,” Lee’s Peter Braus, who repped the buyer, said in a statement. Brandon Polakoff from Avison Young represented the seller, a family LLC doing business as 176 West 87th Leasehold. Polakoff did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Mountain View Acquisition (Friedman's Restaurant group) bought 5,000 SF retail co-op at 541–555 Amsterdam Ave, Manhattan, for $4.1M.
Will open Friedman's Restaurant in vacant unit; Barney Greengrass and Hudson & Charles remain.
Upper West Side retail co-op purchase; 7+ Friedman's locations in Manhattan including Chelsea Market.
stories.summary: The ownership group behind Friedman's Restaurant and Pastrami Queen acquired a 5,000-square-foot retail co-op unit at 541–555 Amsterdam Avenue on Manhattan's Upper West Side for $4.1 million, planning to open a new Friedman's location in the building's vacant space. Existing tenants Barney Greengrass (restaurant and fish vendor) and Hudson & Charles (butcher/sandwich shop) will remain. Friedman's already operates seven+ locations in Manhattan, including its flagship at Chelsea Market.
stories.impact: This is a single-asset retail ground-floor acquisition and restaurant expansion. It reflects Upper West Side retail market stability and consumer demand supporting restaurant growth, but does not directly impact multifamily development supply, demand, or financing. The transaction may signal confidence in Upper West Side foot traffic and renter demographics, indirectly supporting apartment rent growth in the submarket, but carries minimal direct relevance to TCR's development underwriting.

stories.title: Law Firm Thompson Relocates to 4K SF at Cohen Brothers’ 622 Third Avenue
stories.excerpt: This law firm finds its new office very appealing. Thompson, a law firm that specializes in mergers and acquisitions, tax transactions, and intellectual property issues, is relocating its New York City offices to the Cohen Brothers’ 622 Third Avenue, Commercial Observer has learned. The boutique firm signed a five-year, 4,000-square-foot lease on the 16th floor of the 40-story Midtown East office tower, also known as Grand Central Plaza. Thompson will move into its new spot in the fall from its current home at 75 Broad Street in the Financial District. The asking rent was $75 per square foot, according to tenant broker Resolution Real Estate. Resolution’s Jeffrey Zund and Michael Adler represented Thompson on this deal, while Cohen Brothers was represented in-house by Marc Horowitz. Adler, Zund and Horowitz did not immediately respond to CO’s requests for comment. Designed by Emery Roth & Sons, 622 Third Avenue is between East 40th and East 41st streets and underwent a $5 million renovation in the early 2010s. Tenants in the building include employment agency TemPositions, industrial outdoor storage provider Zenith IOS, as well as commercial real estate financing and advisory firm Cooper-Horowitz. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Thompson (M&A/tax/IP law firm) signed 4,000 SF lease at 622 Third Avenue, Midtown East, for 5 years.
Relocated from 75 Broad Street (Financial District); $75/SF asking rent, 16th floor, 40-story tower.
622 Third Avenue underwent $5M renovation early 2010s; Cohen Brothers ownership; Emery Roth & Sons design.
stories.summary: Thompson, a boutique law firm specializing in mergers and acquisitions, tax transactions, and intellectual property, signed a five-year lease for 4,000 square feet on the 16th floor of 622 Third Avenue (Grand Central Plaza) in Midtown East Manhattan at $75 per square foot. The firm is relocating from 75 Broad Street in the Financial District to this 40-story tower owned by Cohen Brothers. The building underwent a $5 million renovation in the early 2010s and is located between East 40th and 41st Streets.
stories.impact: This is a single office tenant lease-up in Midtown East and does not directly signal multifamily demand, supply, or capital conditions. It does suggest modest Midtown East office leasing velocity and that Class A towers are attracting professional services tenants, but provides no material multifamily-relevant information on market rents, job growth, or residential demand in Manhattan.
